      12. Completeness of and pointwise convergence#

      In Note 24 we proved that is a norm on for and a quasinorm for . In Note 1 we saw that the space of continuous functions and the space of Riemann-integrable functions are not complete with respect to the distance: some Cauchy sequences of such functions have no limit within the space, in the same way that a Cauchy sequence of rational numbers may converge to an irrational number. Completeness is the property that allows us to construct an object as the limit of approximations, for instance as the sum of a series, and to know that the limit belongs to the space under study. These notes prove that is complete for every exponent . This theorem is known as the Riesz–Fischer theorem.

      The proof works with the quantity rather than with . Because is the integral of the pointwise quantity , the monotone convergence theorem applies to it directly, and a single quasi-triangle inequality covers all exponents simultaneously. A lemma reduces completeness to the convergence of Cauchy sequences whose consecutive differences satisfy , and for such sequences we construct the limit pointwise, as the sum of a telescoping series.

      The construction produces a limit that is simultaneously an limit and an almost-everywhere limit. In the second part of these notes we compare these two modes of convergence. We prove that convergence with summable errors implies almost-everywhere convergence, deduce that every -convergent sequence has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence, and construct counterexamples showing that neither mode of convergence implies the other in general.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • State the quasi-triangle inequality for with constant and iterate it to bound the -th power of a finite sum.

      • Reduce the convergence of a Cauchy sequence in to the convergence of a subsequence with geometrically decaying consecutive differences.

      • Prove the Riesz–Fischer theorem: is complete for every .

      • Prove that convergence with implies almost-everywhere convergence, and that every -convergent sequence has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence.

      • Construct a sequence that converges in but converges at no point, and sequences that converge everywhere but have no limit in .

      • Apply the dominated convergence theorem to deduce convergence from almost-everywhere convergence.

      Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space, is a fixed exponent, and functions are measurable functions . On subsets of , the symbol denotes Lebesgue measure.

      12.1.2 Reduction to rapidly Cauchy sequences#

      A Cauchy sequence guarantees that is eventually small, but it gives no rate at which this quantity decreases. To build the limit as the sum of the telescoping series , we need consecutive differences that decay at a prescribed geometric rate. The next lemma shows that it is enough to prove convergence for sequences with this rate: every Cauchy sequence has a subsequence with geometrically decaying differences, and a Cauchy sequence converges as soon as one of its subsequences converges.

      12.2 The Riesz–Fischer theorem#

      Theorem 5 (Riesz–Fischer theorem)#

      For every , the space is complete: every Cauchy sequence in converges in to an element of .

      The proof of Theorem 5 established more than convergence. In Step 2, the rapidly Cauchy sequence also converged to almost everywhere. Combined with the subsequence extraction of Lemma 4, this observation shows that every Cauchy sequence in has a subsequence that converges almost everywhere to its limit. The next section examines the relation between convergence and pointwise convergence directly.

      12.3 convergence and pointwise convergence#

      A sequence of functions can approach a limit in two different senses. Almost-everywhere convergence requires at almost every individual point . Convergence in requires the averaged quantity to tend to , and it allows to differ substantially from on sets whose measure tends to . In this section we prove that rapid convergence implies almost-everywhere convergence, and we construct examples showing that neither mode of convergence implies the other in general.
